title: AES
body:
The block cipher everything actually uses. Rijndael, selected by open NIST competition in 2001 to
replace DES, and **the place where [[ABSTRACT ALGEBRA]] stops being a prerequisite on paper and
starts being the thing you are computing in.** Where [[Feistel Network]] hides its algebra inside
lookup tables that were tuned by hand, every AES step is an explicit operation in $GF(2^8)$.

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Block size | 128 bits, always |
| Key size | 128, 192, or 256 bits |
| Rounds | 10, 12, or 14 respectively |
| Structure | substitution-permutation network, **not** Feistel |

The block is a $4\times4$ **state matrix of bytes**, filled column by column. Every round
transforms that matrix.

```
b0  b4  b8  b12
b1  b5  b9  b13
b2  b6  b10 b14
b3  b7  b11 b15
```

## The byte is a field element

This is the fact the whole cipher rests on. A [[Byte]] is an element of $GF(2^8)$, the
[[Finite Field]] with 256 elements, represented as a polynomial of degree $< 8$ over $GF(2)$ with
one bit per coefficient:

$$\texttt{0x53} = 01010011 = x^6 + x^4 + x + 1$$

- **Addition is XOR.** Characteristic 2, so no carries and no subtraction to worry about.
- **Multiplication** is polynomial multiplication reduced modulo the fixed irreducible polynomial
  $x^8 + x^4 + x^3 + x + 1$, so a product of two bytes is a byte again.
- **Every non-zero byte has a multiplicative inverse.** That is what $\mathbb{Z}_{256}$ cannot
  offer, since 2 is a zero divisor there, and it is precisely what the S-box needs. See
  [[Finite Field]] and [[Irreducibility]] for why the quotient by an irreducible polynomial is a
  field at all.

## The four transformations

Each round is ByteSub, ShiftRow, MixColumn, AddRoundKey, in that order. The final round drops
MixColumn.

### ByteSub (SubBytes)

Replace every byte with $b^{-1}$ in $GF(2^8)$ (with $\texttt{0x00}$ mapped to itself), then apply a
fixed affine map over $GF(2)$. This is the **S-box** and the only non-linear step in the cipher:
Shannon's *confusion*, and the reason AES does not collapse to a linear system the way an
[[Stream Cipher|LFSR]] does.

Inversion was chosen because it has the best known resistance to differential and linear
cryptanalysis of any map on a byte, and the affine tail exists to destroy the algebraic
simplicity of pure inversion (which would otherwise fix 0 and 1 and have a compact algebraic
description). Note that this is the same $\texttt{affine}$ word as in [[Classical Ciphers]] and the
same reason: an affine map $x \mapsto ax+b$ over a field is invertible when $a$ is.

In practice the S-box is a 256-byte lookup table, but **the table is computed, not chosen**, and
that is the design argument. DES's S-boxes are a list of numbers you have to trust.

### ShiftRow

Rotate row $i$ left by $i$ bytes. Pure *diffusion*, and a [[Transposition Cipher]] on the state
matrix: nothing changes value, only position. Its job is to move bytes between columns so that the
next step mixes them with different neighbours.

### MixColumn

Treat each column as a 4-vector over $GF(2^8)$ and multiply by a fixed matrix:

$$\begin{pmatrix} 02 & 03 & 01 & 01 \\ 01 & 02 & 03 & 01 \\ 01 & 01 & 02 & 03 \\ 03 & 01 & 01 & 02 \end{pmatrix}$$

This is ordinary matrix-vector multiplication from [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] with the scalars living in
$GF(2^8)$ instead of $\mathbb{R}$, and it is invertible for exactly the usual reason: the matrix has
a non-zero determinant in the field, so an inverse matrix exists. The small entries are chosen so
multiplication is a shift and a conditional XOR rather than a table lookup.

Together ShiftRow and MixColumn give **full diffusion in two rounds**: after two rounds every output
byte depends on every input byte. That is the design target, and the round count is set well above
it for margin.

### AddRoundKey

XOR the state with the round subkey. This is the only step involving the key, and it is where
the [[Symmetric Key Cryptography|one-time-pad]] idea appears: without it the other three steps are a
fixed public permutation and encrypt nothing. The **key schedule** expands the master key into
$rounds + 1$ round keys, using the S-box and round constants so the subkeys are not linear
functions of each other.

## Core facts

- AES is a **substitution-permutation network**, not a Feistel cipher, so decryption needs the
  inverse of each step rather than the same circuit run backwards. That is the cost of dropping
  Feistel, paid for with fewer rounds and full-block diffusion.
- **AES has not been broken.** The best known attacks on full AES-128 improve on brute force by a
  factor of about 4, which is nothing. Real-world AES failures are side-channel (cache timing
  against the S-box table) or mode-related, never algebraic.
- AES-256 exists for margin and for [[Post-Quantum Cryptography|Grover's algorithm]], which halves
  the effective key length of any symmetric cipher, taking 256 bits to a still-fine 128.
- Modern CPUs have `AES-NI` instructions that do a whole round in hardware, so AES is often faster
  than copying the data. See [[Instructions]] for the general idea of a special-purpose opcode.
- **AES encrypts exactly 128 bits.** Encrypting a file requires a [[Modes of Operation|mode]], and
  the mode is where almost every real deployment bug lives.
